Hector. The mightiest warrior of Troy and the tragic heart of the Trojan War. As the eldest son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba, he stood as the supreme commander of all the Trojan forces. He was married to Andromache, a princess from a neighboring kingdom, and father to their young son Astyanax. Deeply devoted to both his family and his city, his love for them motivated his heroic stand against impossible odds. For ten years, Hector defended Troy's walls with both strategic brilliance and personal valor, killing many Greek champions whose reputation alone terrified the Greek forces. One of his greatest deeds came when he slew Patroclus in single combat, not realizing that he was killing Achilles' most beloved companion, a blow that would transform the entire course of the war. When Achilles finally came for him, Hector faced the greatest Greek warrior fully knowing that this would be his last fight, and that Troy could not survive his death. In their climactic duel, though Hector fought with all his valor, he was outmatched by Achilles and fell, pierced through the throat. After his death, Achilles dragged his body around Troy's walls three times as a final indignity, denying him the proper burial rites that were sacred to the Greeks and Trojans alike. Only when Priam himself, the aged king of Troy, humbled himself and begged before his son's killer was Hector's body ransomed, so that he could receive his funeral rites. Both Greeks and Trojans described him as noble, honorable, and devoted to duty, a man whose character was morally superior to many of the Greeks he fought against. Homer portrays Hector as never a villain or savage in the Iliad, but rather as a man worthy of respect even from his enemies. His death symbolized Troy's inevitable doom and the triumph of fate over human effort. His legacy endures across all of Western literature as the archetype of the noble warrior facing unavoidable fate with dignity and courage.
